title: China’s gallium, germanium reprieve gives US time, not certainty
gist: China extended its suspension of the gallium/germanium export ban to the US only to 27 January 2027, keeping licensed non-military sales open, but Benchmark argues the reprieve is near-meaningless in practice: US-bound volumes have been close to zero since 2023 and prices remain ~2.7-2.8x Q4 2025 levels. Ex-China supply diversification (e.g. Atalco's DoW-backed Louisiana gallium project) is growing but leaves both markets reliant on China into the 2030s.

insights.claim: China's Ministry of Commerce extended its suspension of the gallium and germanium export ban to the US to 27 January 2027 — a two-month window, far shorter than the one-year suspension agreed after the Trump–Xi Busan meeting.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Short rolling deadlines keep minor-metal supply hostage to US–China negotiation cycles; watch the late-January 2027 decision as a volatility catalyst.

insights.claim: China's gallium/germanium export-ban reprieve closely mirrors its rare earth export pause, which was extended only to 10 January, suggesting Beijing is synchronising critical-mineral levers on short leashes.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Treat China's critical-mineral pauses as a linked bargaining bundle — a breakdown in one likely spills into the others.
insights.quote: the shorter window closely reflects China’s rare earth pause, extended to 10 January

insights.claim: Even under China's suspension, gallium and germanium exports to US military end users remain banned and every shipment still requires a licence, as it has since August 2023.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Defense supply chains get no relief from the reprieve; domestic/allied sourcing for military electronics stays a priority funding area.

insights.claim: Gallium metal (99.99%, CIF Europe) fell 9% to $3,150/kg on 26 November 2026 from $3,450/kg two weeks earlier but remains about 2.8x the Q4 2025 ex-China average; prices had already started softening before China's extension announcement.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Ex-China gallium is easing but still carries a large scarcity premium; the extension was not itself a bearish price catalyst.

insights.claim: Germanium metal (99.999%, CIF Europe) held flat at $15,500/kg in late November 2026, about 2.7x its Q4 2025 average, indicating China's extension did little to change market sentiment.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Germanium-dependent sectors (optics, IR, semis) face sustained elevated input costs regardless of the reprieve.

insights.claim: China's unwrought gallium exports fell 94% in 2025 and had not recovered in early 2026, while recorded gallium/germanium shipments to the US have been close to zero since 2023 — so China's licensing reprieve has delivered little real volume to US buyers.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Headline policy relief does not equal physical supply; US buyers should be modelled as effectively cut off from Chinese Ga/Ge.
insights.locator: The metal exists but is not reaching the US

insights.claim: A Europe-based minor metals trader reports that US licence attempts for Chinese gallium/germanium have failed either on US-side compliance grounds or due to Chinese military-use restrictions, so the US has received effectively no Ga or Ge in over three years.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Friction exists on both sides of the licence process — even a broader Chinese opening would not quickly restore US flows.
insights.quote: any licence attempt has either failed on the US side due to compliance reasons or due to Chinese restrictions on military uses
insights.locator: I see little to no impact from this

insights.claim: Benchmark's Head of Strategic Initiatives Mike Finch argues the two-month gallium/germanium reprieve does nothing for long-term supply-security confidence, so buyers will keep prioritising supply-chain diversification whatever Beijing decides in January.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Sustained procurement demand for ex-China Ga/Ge sources supports offtake-backed projects outside China.
insights.quote: a two-month extension is unlikely to move the needle
insights.locator: This is a reprieve for non-military consumers

insights.claim: Benchmark estimates China's 2026 gallium surplus at 275t against an ex-China shortfall of 182t, and China's germanium surplus at 53t against a 52t ex-China gap, before trade — base cases that assume licensing continues at 2026 export volumes through next year.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: The global market is not short of metal, only of non-Chinese metal — pricing is a geography/policy spread, vulnerable to any change in licensing volumes.
insights.locator: Benchmark’s Gallium Service puts China’s 2026 surplus

insights.claim: Ex-China primary gallium supply is forecast to rise from 10t in 2026 to more than 200t by 2030, helped by government funding such as the US Department of War's $400m commitment to Atalco's Louisiana project.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Government-backed ex-China gallium capacity (Atalco) is the key supply-response vehicle to track; a 20x ramp could compress the ex-China premium by 2030.
insights.locator: Diversification is under way, but slowly

insights.claim: Ex-China primary germanium supply is forecast to nearly double from 45t to 84t, yet both the gallium and germanium markets will remain reliant on Chinese material, to a lesser extent, into the next decade.
insights.speaker: Michael Finch, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: China retains structural leverage over Ga/Ge well into the 2030s; diversification reduces but does not remove the geopolitical risk premium.
insights.locator: Diversification is under way, but slowly
